answer.text: The spring parade in Ana's city and the harvest fair in Tom's town are quite different, but both are lively. The parade is far more crowded than the fair: thousands of people come to see the colourful costumes and listen to loud music. The parade is also noticeably older; it is about two hundred years old, whereas the fair is only fifty. In both places, families tend to spend the day together and share food. answer.text: Mia opened the kitchen door slowly. It creaked, and a faint scent of burnt toast filled the room. The kitchen was dim and damp, and somebody had left a cup of tea on the table. It was still warm. 'Who was here?' Mia whispered, and a shiver ran down her back. She had heard footsteps in the garden earlier, but she had told nobody. Then she noticed that the window was open. 'Grandma?' she called. 'It is only me,' a voice muttered from the dark corner. Grandma was sitting in her old chair, and she had not slept for two nights.
accepted: Mia opened the kitchen door slowly. It creaked, and a faint scent of burnt toast filled the room. The kitchen was dim and damp, and somebody had left a cup of tea on the table. It was still warm. 'Who was here?' Mia whispered, and a shiver ran down her back. She had heard footsteps in the garden earlier, but she had told nobody. Then she noticed that the window was open. 'Grandma?' she called. 'It is only me,' a voice muttered from the dark corner. Grandma was sitting in her old chair, and she had not slept for two nights.

Mia entered her grandmother's kitchen at midnight. The floor creaked, and a faint smell of coffee hung in the air. The room was dim, and someone had left the back door open. 'Who is there?' Mia whispered. Nobody answered. She glanced at the table: a cup of tea was still warm, so somebody had been there minutes before. 'Come out,' she snapped, although her hands were cold. Then a shiver ran down her back, because she had heard the same footsteps the night before. Finally a voice muttered, 'Do not shout, it is only me.' Grandma had come down for a glass of water.

When Mia opened the door, it creaked loudly. The kitchen was dim, and a faint scent of smoke filled the air. Someone had left a cup of tea on the table, and it was still warm. 'Is anybody here?' Mia whispered. Nothing moved. She glanced at the window, which was open, and a shiver ran down her back. She had locked it before dinner, she was sure. 'Stop hiding,' she snapped. Then Grandma appeared at the door and muttered that she had only wanted some fresh air.

answer.text:
Hi Carlos,

I am writing to give you an update on the volunteer guide. So far, I have completed three of the five sections, and the project is on track overall, although we are slightly behind on the last two sections.

The main obstacle has been a delay in the photos from the school. Without them, I cannot finish the sections about the garden and the library, and I have not been able to start the layout. I have already written to the school twice, but nobody has replied yet.

Meanwhile, I will be writing the two remaining sections, so they are ready as soon as the photos arrive. Next week I will also be testing the guide with two volunteers, and I will be collecting their comments. I will send you a short summary of their feedback on Friday.

I would be grateful if you could contact the school and ask them to send the photos by Wednesday. With your support, I am sure we can still finish on time.

Thank you very much for your help.

Best wishes,
Sara

prompt.es: Escribe la transcripción de tu charla de dos minutos (unas 170–210 palabras).

answer.text:
Have you ever tried to sleep while the traffic never stops outside your window? Today I will outline two ideas about noise in our city: why it is growing, and what we can do about it.

Firstly, let me explain why it is growing. Here is one statistic that surprised me: the number of cars in our city has doubled in ten years. Every new car adds more noise to our streets, and the noise does not stop at night. Moreover, the impact on our health is bigger than most people think. Noise makes us tired and nervous, and it makes it hard to concentrate at school or at work.

Secondly, what can we do? We can walk or cycle to school, we can ask the council for quiet zones, and we can talk to our neighbours about the problem. Who will make our city quieter if we do not? The council? The police? Or you and me?

To wrap up, let me recap my two ideas. The noise is growing because of traffic, and it harms our health. My takeaway is simple: small changes can make a quiet city. Thank you for listening, and I am happy to take your questions.

answer.text:
Have you ever walked past a dirty park and thought: somebody should do something? Today I will outline two ideas: the problem and a simple solution, a monthly cleaning day run by students.

Firstly, let me show you the problem. Here is one statistic that surprised me: every week, our school throws away more than two hundred kilos of paper. Last year, the park near our school was dirty for months, and nobody cleaned it. Think about the cost too: all the paper that we throw away is money that we could spend on new books.

Secondly, what can we do? I propose one Saturday a month, four groups of volunteers and two hours of work. Some people say that nobody will come, but other schools already do the same, and it works. Moreover, the impact would be bigger than the work itself: students would learn to take responsibility, and our neighbours would see that young people care. Yesterday the park was dirty; today we can make it clean. Who will do it if we do not? The council? The teachers? Or you and me?

To wrap up, let me recap my two ideas: the problem is real, and the solution is simple. My takeaway is this: a clean park begins with one Saturday. Thank you for listening, and I am happy to take your questions.

prompt.es: Escribe un párrafo con tres pistas, una conclusión y una alternativa descartada.

answer.text: The bakery has been closed for five days, and there are three clues. First, there is a delivery van at the door. Second, the front has new paint. Third, someone saw the owner with a new sign yesterday. These clues suggest that the bakery is not closing for good: it is probably having a renovation or moving to a bigger place. Of course, each clue on its own is weak, but together they make a strong case. We can rule out the alternative that the owner has left, because of the new sign. I will ask him tomorrow to be sure.
accepted: The bakery has been closed for five days, and there are three clues. First, there is a delivery van at the door. Second, the front has new paint. The bakery has been shut for five days. I can see a van outside, fresh paint on the wall and a new sign in the owner's hand. Together, these clues point to a renovation, although I may be wrong. The cleaner has a key and came yesterday, so the cleaner must have moved the trophy. I can't be completely sure, so we should ask the cleaner first.

answer.text: On a rainy Saturday the market was a grey river. People moved between the stalls like leaves in the water, and the rain danced on the roofs and whispered to the fruit. The lamps were golden apples in the dark morning, and the whole place breathed warm air. I chose the river because it shows how the crowd never stops moving. accepted: On a rainy Saturday the market was a grey river. People moved between the stalls like leaves in the water, and the rain danced on the roofs and whispered to the fruit. The lamps were golden apples in the dark morning, and the whole place breathed warm air. I chose the river because it shows how the crowd never stops moving. The sellers called their prices, and the smell of bread and coffee made everybody smile. It was a noisy, colourful place, and I felt happy and small in the middle of it, like a small boat on the river.

Yesterday the market was a big kitchen on a rainy day. The sellers shouted like cooks, and the crowd moved as slowly as a river between the stalls. The rain danced on the umbrellas and sang a quiet song. The fruit looked like small lamps, red and yellow and green. The smell of bread and coffee was a warm hug for everybody. I chose the kitchen because it shows how warm and busy the place was, even when the sky was grey. Everybody was wet, but everybody was smiling, and the market kept breathing until the evening.

answer.text: Learning English is a long journey. At the beginning, I was at the door with no map, and I felt lost. Grammar became my map, and vocabulary became my compass. Every class was a step, and every mistake was a turn in the road that showed me a new way. Sometimes the road was long and sometimes I walked slowly, but I never stopped. Now I can understand songs, films and conversations, and I am not afraid of wrong turns. Looking back, the journey taught me that patience matters more than speed. One day I will reach my destination, but the road itself is already a good place to live.
accepted: Learning English is a long journey. At the beginning, I was at the door with no map, and I felt lost. Grammar became my map, and vocabulary became my compass. Every class was a step, and every mistake was a turn in the road that showed me a new way. Sometimes the road was long and sometimes I walked slowly, but I never stopped. Now I can understand songs, films and conversations, and I am not afraid of wrong turns. Looking back, the journey taught me that patience matters more than speed. One day I will reach my destination, but the road itself is already a good place to live.

Learning English is a garden. On the first day I planted a few words, and every morning I watered them with a little practice. Some words grew quickly, and others needed more time, but I never stopped planting. Grammar was the ground, and my mistakes were the bad plants that I took out one by one. My teacher was a patient gardener, and my friends were the sun. Sometimes it was hard, and I felt lost in the garden. Looking back, the garden taught me that patience matters more than speed. Today I have a few flowers, and I am happy, but I will keep planting new words every day.

answer.text: In the scene at the station, an old woman waits alone on a bench. A young man sits next to her and gives her a letter that she lost many years ago. She looks at the envelope, touches it and says nothing for ten seconds. Then she smiles. What makes this moment so moving is the silence: nobody speaks, but we understand everything. It is the small detail of her hands that conveys her feelings, because they shake a little when she touches the letter. The performance is understated, and the pace is slow, which gives the scene its tension. Overall, I think this is the best moment of the film because it suggests a whole life without a single line of dialogue. It is a turning point, and the audience feels the truth before the woman says a word.

In the final scene, a boy opens the door of an empty house and freezes. A letter lies on the floor. He reads it slowly, and his face changes. What I liked most was the silence, because nobody explains the moment. It is the music that builds the tension, and it stops at the perfect second. The acting is understated: he says nothing, but his eyes show everything. Overall, the scene is gripping and moving because it trusts the audience. It suggests more than it tells, and that is why it is the turning point of the story. I would watch it again just for this moment.

origin.text:
HOST: Welcome back to Tech Talk. Today our topic is phones in the classroom. Our guest is Sara, a teacher and researcher. Sara, should schools ban phones?
GUEST: I do not think so. A phone is a strong tool: students can search for information, use a dictionary and take notes.
HOST: But many students use their phones to play games or chat with friends.
GUEST: That is true, and I admit that it is a problem. Even so, I suggest using phones only for clear tasks and putting them away when the task is finished.
HOST: Some parents worry that children will become tired and anxious.
GUEST: I understand. The research points out that too much screen time affects sleep, so I warn students not to use their phones late at night.
HOST: I am still not sure. I think a full ban is easier to control.
GUEST: A ban is easy, but it does not teach self-control. I recommend trying a three-month test in one school.
HOST: Interesting. Before we go, thank you, Sara. That is all for today.

answer.text: I remember standing on my grandmother's porch on hot summer evenings. The air was warm, and the scent of fresh bread came from the kitchen. I can still hear the creak of the old gate and the echo of my cousins laughing in the garden. I will never forget watching the sun go down behind the hills while she told us stories. One evening, I forgot to say goodbye when my parents took me home, and I still regret not hugging her that night. Now I must remember to call her every Sunday. Sometimes I close my eyes, and that porch is there again, small and golden, exactly as it was. Some memories stay vivid for ever.
accepted: I remember standing on my grandmother's porch on hot summer evenings. The air was warm, and the scent of fresh bread came from the kitchen. I can still hear the creak of the old gate and the echo of my cousins laughing in the garden. I will never forget watching the sun go down behind the hills while she told us stories. One evening, I forgot to say goodbye when my parents took me home, and I still regret not hugging her that night. Now I must remember to call her every Sunday. Sometimes I close my eyes, and that porch is there again, small and golden, exactly as it was. Some memories stay vivid for ever.

I remember playing in my grandfather's garden every summer. The air was warm, and the scent of apples was everywhere. I can still hear the creak of the wooden gate and the echo of his voice calling us for dinner. I will never forget eating under the big tree while he told funny stories. I regret not asking him more questions about his life, and I must remember to visit his house again this year. When I close my eyes, that garden comes back, small and green and full of light. It is a vivid memory that I do not want to forget.

answer.text: Dear Tom, thank you for your post. I take your point about sleep, and I would not deny that many teenagers are tired in the morning. Nonetheless, I do not think a later start is the best answer. First, the evidence is not clear: one school changed its timetable, but the grades stayed the same. With respect, one example is not enough to change every school. Second, while a later start could help students sleep, it would also end the day later. Many students have sports, jobs or lessons after school, and their parents cannot always collect them. Buses would also need new timetables, and that would cost the council more money. I agree that students should rest, but perhaps the school could start a little later, at half past eight, and keep the day the same length. In conclusion, I accept that sleep matters, yet I believe a smaller change would solve the problem without creating new ones. Best wishes, Ana

answer.text: Thank you, chair. My position is clear: the city centre should be closed to cars, for three reasons. First, the air is dirty, and children breathe it every day. Second, the streets are narrow, and cyclists and pedestrians are not safe. Third, the centre can be a place where people walk, shop and meet. Granted, some shops are worried, and I would not deny that deliveries are a real difficulty. Nonetheless, the evidence from other cities is encouraging. Visitors stay longer on pedestrian streets, hence the rise in sales reported by several shops. The council could also create a scheme whereby delivery vans enter before nine in the morning, thereby protecting both business and safety. With respect, a few parking spaces are a small price for cleaner air and safer streets. On balance, I believe the plan helps residents, visitors and shops. To sum up, we should protect the centre for people, not for cars. Thank you.

Good evening, everyone. I am against closing the whole centre to cars, and I have two main reasons. First, many older residents and sick people need to arrive by car. Second, shops need deliveries and customers who come from outside the city. Admittedly, the air in the centre is not clean, and I take your point about cyclists and pedestrians. Be that as it may, a full ban is too strict. The council could create a scheme whereby only electric vehicles enter at certain hours, thereby reducing pollution without closing the streets. answer.text: Many students believe that long study nights are the best way to prepare for exams, but research suggests that regular short sessions may be more effective. A survey of 200 college students found that those who studied for forty minutes every day scored ten percent higher than those who studied only before the exam. This appears to show that regular review helps memory, although the effect may depend on the subject. For example, languages and science seem to benefit more from daily practice than essay subjects. It could be argued that students who study every day are simply more interested in studying, so the results should be read with care. To a certain extent, a good schedule matters more than the number of hours. In conclusion, a short session every day is likely to be a better habit than one long night, but more research is needed.
accepted: Many students believe that long study nights are the best way to prepare for exams, but research suggests that regular short sessions may be more effective. A survey of 200 college students found that those who studied for forty minutes every day scored ten percent higher than those who studied only before the exam. This appears to show that regular review helps memory, although the effect may depend on the subject. For example, languages and science seem to benefit more from daily practice than essay subjects. It could be argued that students who study every day are simply more interested in studying, so the results should be read with care. To a certain extent, a good schedule matters more than the number of hours. In conclusion, a short session every day is likely to be a better habit than one long night, but more research is needed.

Some people think that listening to music while studying improves concentration. However, a study of 120 teenagers suggests that silence may be better for difficult tasks. The teenagers who worked in a quiet room scored eight percent higher on a reading test than those who listened to music. This seems to indicate that music can distract students, although it might help with simple tasks such as copying notes. It could be argued that some students are used to music and feel calmer with it, so the effect may depend on the person. Largely for this reason, the results should be read with care. Nevertheless, there is some evidence that a quiet schedule with short sessions is likely to work better for most students.

answer.text: Good morning, everyone. Let me summarise our study. One hundred and fifty students kept a study diary for a month. The students who reviewed their notes every day scored twelve percent higher in a final test than the others. The findings suggest that daily review may help students remember more, and this seems to be true for most subjects. Some of you may have an objection, so let me reply to one of them: a classmate said that these students were probably more interested already. That is a fair point, and it is a limitation of the study. To a certain extent, you may be right. Nevertheless, the difference was large, and it is likely to be valid for students of our age. More research is needed before we can be sure, but I would suggest trying daily review this month. Thank you for listening.
accepted: Good morning, everyone. Let me summarise our study. One hundred and fifty students kept a study diary for a month. The findings suggest that daily review may help students remember more, and this seems to be true for most subjects. Some of you may have an objection, so let me reply to one of them: a classmate said that these students were probably more interested already. That is a fair point, and it is a limitation of the study. To a certain extent, you may be right. Nevertheless, the difference was large, and it is likely to be valid for students of our age. More research is needed before we can be sure, but I would suggest trying daily review this month. Thank you for listening.

Hello, everyone. To summarise, 150 students wrote in a study diary every day for a month. After the month, the students who reviewed their notes daily scored twelve percent higher in the final test. The results suggest that regular review might improve memory. Someone has asked whether these students were already more interested. That is a good point, and I accept it as a limitation. It could be argued that interested students simply study more. However, the findings still seem to show a clear effect, so I think the conclusion is likely to be valid, although we need more research. For now, I would suggest that we all try daily review for one month, and then compare our scores. Thank you for your attention.

Roughly half of them are first-year students, and nearly a third are boys. This suggests that the club is becoming more popular, and it may grow even more next year. Finally, let me tell you about our plan. We would like to organise a reading night in June and invite two other schools. To sum up, the club started small, grew steadily and is ready for a new challenge. Thank you for listening. I am happy to answer any questions.

Hello, everyone, and welcome. Today I want to present my hobby, which is running, and I will outline the talk in three parts: why I started, how my training changed and my next goal. Firstly, I started running two years ago because I wanted to feel healthier. At the beginning, I could run for only ten minutes without stopping. Let's move on to the second part: my training. As you can see in my chart, my weekly distance rose gradually, from roughly five to around twenty kilometres in one year. I also take a short pause between exercises, and I keep a steady pace. Now I'd like to turn to my goal for next year. I am likely to run a half marathon in the spring, and my friends will run with me. To sum up, running is cheap, simple and good for the head as well as for the body. Thank you very much for listening. Are there any questions?

A man was sleeping on a bench, and there was a small clock above the ticket office. I felt cold and afraid. What I remember most is the silence, which was like a wall between me and the rest of the city. I took out my phone, but my phone had no power. Then I heard a voice behind me. It was my old teacher who was standing there with an umbrella! She had seen me from the bus and had followed me inside. She laughed, gave me her phone and said, “Call Sara. She has probably been waiting for you.” I called, and Sara answered at once. She was not angry. In fact, she had missed the train too, and she was waiting at the next station. My teacher bought us all a hot drink while we waited for the next train. We talked about the long day, about our families and about the rain. We met Sara an hour later, and we laughed about the whole night. I will never forget how kind both of them were.
accepted: It was raining when I reached the station, and my bag was heavy. I had promised Sara that I would be there at eight, but the last train had already left. The station was almost empty. A man was sleeping on a bench, and there was a small clock above the ticket office. I felt cold and afraid. What I remember most is the silence, which was like a wall between me and the rest of the city. I took out my phone, but my phone had no power. Then I heard a voice behind me. It was my old teacher who was standing there with an umbrella! She had seen me from the bus and had followed me inside. She laughed, gave me her phone and said, “Call Sara. She has probably been waiting for you.” I called, and Sara answered at once. She was not angry. In fact, she had missed the train too, and she was waiting at the next station. My teacher bought us all a hot drink while we waited for the next train. We talked about the long day, about our families and about the rain. We met Sara an hour later, and we laughed about the whole night. I will never forget how kind both of them were.

It was getting dark when I arrived at the cinema, and a long line was waiting outside. I had bought the tickets two days before, but when I looked in my bag, I understood that I had left them at home. My heart was beating like a drum. What I felt most was shame, because Leo had already told everyone that the film was his idea. I walked to the desk and explained the problem. The woman smiled and said, “Do not worry. Show me the message on your phone.” I looked for it, but my hands were shaking. Finally I found it. It was a small miracle that the message was still there! She checked the name, printed two new tickets and wished us a good film. When I found Leo, the film had already started, so we sat in the dark and whispered like children. Afterwards we walked home and he laughed at me all the way. I remember that night as the day I learned to check my bag twice, and I also remember the woman at the desk, who was kinder than I deserved.

answer.text: Thank you, everyone. I would like to propose a street market on the first Sunday of each month, with stalls for local food and plants. It would bring neighbours together and help small businesses. Tom, I take your point: admittedly, a market may be noisy, and we do not have much money. However, I see it a little differently. With respect, I think the noise would last only a few hours, and the stall fees could pay for the cleaning. I'm afraid I cannot agree that the risk is so big. Could we agree to try it for one month and then review the noise and the cost together? If it does not work, we will stop. Shall we say that we start in October and meet again in November?

With respect, I think the noise would last only a few hours, and the stall fees could pay for the cleaning. I'm afraid I cannot agree that the risk is so big. Could we agree to try it for one month and then review the noise and the cost together? If it does not work, we will stop. Shall we say that we start in October and meet again in November?

Good evening. I'd like to suggest closing our street to cars on one Sunday a month for a small market. It is true that it could be loud, Tom, and I understand your worry about the budget. Still, I am not sure that the problem is as big as it seems. The stalls would pay a small fee, and volunteers could help clean the street afterwards. What if we agree to a one-month test? Perhaps we could meet again afterwards and decide together whether the market should continue. I believe this is fair for everyone, and I hope you agree.

answer.text: I firmly believe that our city should close its centre streets to cars on Sundays. First, a car-free centre would be safer, especially for children and older people. It would also be quieter, so families could walk, talk and enjoy the shops. It is true that some drivers may find it inconvenient, and some shops could lose a few customers. To some extent, I understand that worry. However, it seems that more people would come on foot, and they would spend time and money in the centre. On the other hand, we could keep one street open for deliveries and for people who cannot walk far. In short, a car-free Sunday would make our centre safer, calmer and friendlier, and I believe the benefits outweigh the costs.
accepted: I firmly believe that our city should close its centre streets to cars on Sundays. First, a car-free centre would be safer, especially for children and older people. It would also be quieter, so families could walk, talk and enjoy the shops. It is true that some drivers may find it inconvenient, and some shops could lose a few customers. To some extent, I understand that worry. However, it seems that more people would come on foot, and they would spend time and money in the centre. On the other hand, we could keep one street open for deliveries and for people who cannot walk far. In short, a car-free Sunday would make our centre safer, calmer and friendlier, and I believe the benefits outweigh the costs.

My position is clear: the streets of the centre should be closed to traffic on Sundays. Admittedly, it may be difficult for people who live far away, and I agree that the plan needs good buses. Perhaps the city could add a free bus on those days. Even so, I am convinced that the change would help. Children could play, people could meet, and the air would probably be cleaner. Some say shops would suffer, but it seems that busy streets usually bring more customers. To sum up, a quiet Sunday centre would be a great gift to everyone, and I think it is worth a try.

answer.text: Hi Sam, thank you for your message. I think you are saying that the cleaning is not shared fairly, and I understand why you feel that way. It is true that I have been out a lot this month, and I admit that some weeks you have done more than your part. However, I firmly believe the problem is partly my work schedule, because I finish late on most days and I am often too tired to clean. Hello Sam, thanks for telling me how you feel. Your message suggests that I am not doing enough, and I can see why you are upset. Admittedly, I have not cleaned much lately, and I am sorry about that. Still, my new job means that I work late most evenings, so perhaps the real problem is time, not effort. prompt.es: Escribe una anécdota de 160 a 210 palabras con hábito, giro y consecuencia.

answer.text: In those days, my grandfather and I used to fish at the lake every Sunday. He would bring a bottle of tea, and we would sit in silence for hours. Gradually, I noticed that his hands were shaking, but he never mentioned it. Meanwhile, I was busy with school and my friends, and I did not ask any questions. One Sunday, he did not come to the door. I waited for twenty minutes, and my hands were cold. Then I saw the light in the kitchen. He was sitting at the table, pale and quiet, with our fishing things beside him. 'I cannot walk to the lake any more,' he said. I froze. I had never seen him sad. Eventually, I sat next to him, and we drank the tea together, without fishing. Since that day, I have visited him every Sunday, and we talk instead of fishing. Looking back, I think that quiet morning taught me more than all our years at the lake.
accepted: In those days, my grandfather and I used to fish at the lake every Sunday. He would bring a bottle of tea, and we would sit in silence for hours. Gradually, I noticed that his hands were shaking, but he never mentioned it. Meanwhile, I was busy with school and my friends, and I did not ask any questions. One Sunday, he did not come to the door. I waited for twenty minutes, and my hands were cold. Then I saw the light in the kitchen. He was sitting at the table, pale and quiet, with our fishing things beside him. 'I cannot walk to the lake any more,' he said. I froze. I had never seen him sad. Eventually, I sat next to him, and we drank the tea together, without fishing. Since that day, I have visited him every Sunday, and we talk instead of fishing. Looking back, I think that quiet morning taught me more than all our years at the lake.

In those days, I would walk home along the river every evening, after my classes. Gradually, the path became darker, because the lights went out one by one. Meanwhile, I was thinking about my exam and I did not notice the silence. Then I heard steps behind me. My heart stopped. I turned around slowly, and I saw a small dog with a red bottle in its mouth. Eventually, I laughed so much that I had to sit down. Since that night, I always carry some bread in my pocket, just in case. Looking back, I think that night taught me to laugh at my own fear.

feedback.es: La anécdota combina fondo habitual, marcadores de secuencia, un giro con suspense, la consecuencia y una reflexión final.

answer.text: Fifty years ago, my grandmother missed the last bus the night before her wedding. She was alone on a dark road, and it started to rain. Then a farmer stopped and offered her a lift. She arrived at dawn, tired and muddy, but she reached the church on time. The lesson? Sometimes help comes from the people you least expect. Was she worried? Terribly, but she kept walking. Did he wait for her? Of course! My grandfather was standing at the church door, and they stayed together for fifty years.
accepted: Fifty years ago, my grandmother missed the last bus the night before her wedding. She was alone on a dark road, and it started to rain. Then a farmer stopped and offered her a lift. Did he wait for her? Of course! My grandfather was standing at the church door, and they stayed together for fifty years.

My grandmother always tells us about the night before her wedding. She missed the last bus, and she had to walk in the rain. Suddenly, a farmer stopped his car and gave her a lift, so she got home at dawn. Was she worried? Yes, but she kept calm. Did he wait for her? Of course! answer.text: The panel asked me five questions. First, they wanted to know why I wanted the scholarship, and I explained my motivation. Second, I was asked to describe a time when I led a project. Third, they enquired about my plans for July and wanted to know whether I could travel. Then, they asked what I would do if the group did not agree. Finally, I was asked to name one weakness. Overall, I felt confident and calm during the interview. On reflection, my second answer was the best because it had a clear example. Next time I aim to improve my answer to the hypothetical question by adding a reason.

I had an interview for the scholarship, and the panel asked me five questions. They wanted to know why I wanted the scholarship, and then I was asked to describe a time when I led a project. They also enquired about July and asked if I could travel. After that, they wanted to know what I would do if the group did not agree, and I was asked to name one weakness. answer.text:
Dear Ana and Leo,
Thank you both for talking openly today. Let me summarise what I heard. Ana, it sounds like you feel overwhelmed when the Sunday plans change at the last minute, and you need to know earlier. Leo, what I'm hearing is that you feel left out when you cannot see your friends, and you need some free time. Neither of you is wrong: you both want a calm weekend and to feel respected.
What if we try a compromise? Leo will tell Ana by Friday evening if he has other plans. Ana will keep Sunday lunch free until then, and she will not ask him to cancel later. If either of you feels upset, please say it with an I-message, for example, I feel frustrated when...
So we agreed that we will follow this plan for two weeks. Let's review it next Sunday, and we can change anything that does not work.
Thank you both for your honesty and your patience. I am proud of how you listened to each other, and I hope that this small plan helps you to enjoy your Sundays again.
Mia

answer.text:
Team, sit down for a moment. I know this defeat hurts, and it is fine to feel disappointed. I feel the same.
First, I want to say what I saw. Despite the defeat, I'm proud of how you defended in the second half. Mia, your two tackles saved us three times, and Tom, you never stopped talking to the team. That is what a real captain does.
However, we lost the ball too often in the middle of the pitch, and that gave them the chance to score. It is only one thing, and it is fixable. One match does not decide our season.
So let me ask you: what would it take for us to keep the ball longer next Saturday? What could we try in training on Thursday? I would like to hear two ideas from each of you.
Remember, you deserve credit for your effort today. Go home, rest, and come back ready to learn. I believe in this team.

Everyone, come here. I know how painful this defeat is, and I understand you are disappointed. I am too.
I want to start with what worked. I'm proud of how you supported each other during the last twenty minutes. Leo, your effort in defence was excellent, and Sara, you encouraged everybody until the final whistle.

Now, what would help us to use the whole field next week? What is stopping us from looking for the right side? What could we try first on Tuesday? Think about it tonight, and tell me tomorrow.
It was a tough day, but you deserve to be proud of your effort. We will bounce back, and I will be with you on Saturday.

prompt.es: Escribe el anuncio del cambio a los voluntarios.

answer.text:
Hi everyone,
Thank you for coming. I want to announce a change in our Saturday schedule. The reason is simple: more families are coming to the garden, and we need more time to help them.
Here is the plan. First, we will have two shifts instead of one: nine to twelve, and twelve to three. Second, each volunteer will choose a shift by Friday. Third, we will review the plan in a month.
We will support you with a clear guide and a buddy for your first week. Nobody will work alone.
Tom, I understand your concern about the early start. It sounds like you feel stressed because you study at night. What would make the afternoon shift easier for you?
Ana, I hear that you are worried about the new register. What would help you feel more confident? I can practise it with you on Thursday.
I know change is tough, but I am proud of what this team does every week. Thank you for your effort, and please tell me what you think.

Dear volunteers,
I want to announce a change for Saturdays. The reason is that many more families are coming to the garden, and our morning is now too short.
This is the plan. We will work in two shifts, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. Each of you can choose the shift that suits you best. We will review the schedule after four weeks, and then we will decide together if we keep it.
Of course, we will support you. You will receive a short guide, and an experienced volunteer will help you during the first week.
Tom, I understand your concern. You study at night, so the early start is hard. What would make the afternoon shift possible for you?
Ana, it sounds like you feel worried about the new register. What could we try so that you feel more confident? I am happy to practise it with you.
Change is never easy, but your effort makes a real difference. Thank you for your patience and your ideas.

answer.text: Hi Kenji, sorry about that. Those are idioms. “Back to square one” means we have to start again from the beginning. When Leo said the price was too high, he hit the nail on the head, because it was exactly the problem. In other words, the first idiom is about starting again and the second is about being exactly right. Does that make sense? I can also write without idioms next time, so please tell me if any other phrase is unclear. I will explain it in simple words. Thank you for asking!

origin.text: Community gardens are growing fast in European cities. In the last ten years, thousands of neighbours have started to grow vegetables together on small plots of public land. answer.text: I still remember the night I missed the last train. I was a student, and I had spent the whole evening at a friend's birthday party in the next town. When I reached the station, the platform was empty and the clock showed midnight. My phone had no battery, and the nearest taxi was far away. I sat on a cold bench and tried to stay calm. It was not the dark that frightened me; it was the silence. Never had I heard a city so quiet. Then, behind me, I heard footsteps. They were slow, and they were coming closer. I held my bag tightly and did not look back. 'Are you waiting for the last train?' a voice asked. I looked up, and my heart stopped. The man in front of me was wearing a long grey coat, and he looked strangely familiar. He turned out to be Mr Duarte, my new science teacher, who lived two streets away. He smiled, offered me a lift and even gave me his phone charger. All the way home I kept thinking about how afraid I had been of a person who only wanted to help. Looking back, I realise that the real problem was not the empty station. It was my habit of expecting the worst and of staying silent when I needed help. Since that night, I ask for help earlier, and I listen for the kind voice before I imagine the dangerous one.

The night I missed the last train began like any other. I was at a party in the next town, and I left too late. On the platform, the clock showed midnight and nobody was there. I sat down and waited, because my phone had no battery. What frightened me most was the silence. Then I heard footsteps behind me, slow and close. I did not dare to look. The lights were weak, and the wind moved some old paper along the ground. A voice said, 'Are you waiting for the last train?' I looked up, and there was my new science teacher, Mr Duarte, in a long grey coat. It turned out that he lived nearby, and he offered me a lift home. In the car we hardly spoke, but it was warm, and the radio played softly. I felt almost ashamed. I had been afraid of a man who only wanted to help. Looking back, I learned that I often expect the worst when I am alone. Never again will I stay silent when I need help.

Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My uncle Tom would always tell the same story about his first car. That year, he was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden. Nobody recognised him. Silence. answer.text: In my family, Sunday lunch is a custom that we have had for many years. By and large, relatives tend to arrive around noon, and a visitor is always welcome to join us. For example, last week my cousin brought a friend from Japan, and we simply added one more chair. We usually share one big dish from the centre of the table. In some countries people eat from separate plates, whereas in mine we like to pass the food around. Neither way is better; each tradition makes sense at home. It may seem unusual at first, but visitors quickly feel at home because everybody talks, laughs and asks questions. I hope you will join us one Sunday, and I promise to explain every custom with a smile.
accepted: In my family, Sunday lunch is a custom that we have had for many years. By and large, relatives tend to arrive around noon, and a visitor is always welcome to join us. For example, last week my cousin brought a friend from Japan, and we simply added one more chair. We usually share one big dish from the centre of the table. In some countries people eat from separate plates, whereas in mine we like to pass the food around. Neither way is better; each tradition makes sense at home. It may seem unusual at first, but visitors quickly feel at home because everybody talks, laughs and asks questions. I hope you will join us one Sunday, and I promise to explain every custom with a smile.

Every Friday my family has pizza night, a tradition we started when I was a child. As a rule, everybody is home by seven, and the children tend to choose what we eat. For instance, my little brother always asks for cheese and tomato, and we all laugh. Visitors are welcome too, and they usually bring a dessert. In other countries families often eat at the table, whereas in mine we sit on the sofa and watch a film. Neither way is wrong; it is simply a different habit. At first it may feel a bit strange, but guests normally relax after the first bite. I would love to have you with us one Friday, and I promise to share the best part.

answer.text: In my view, pupils should clean their classroom once a week. Admittedly, it takes time away from lessons, and some parents will say that cleaning is the job of the school. That is a reasonable point, but what matters is the habit we build. It is the pupils who use the room every day, and it is undoubtedly fairer that all of us look after it. I believe pupils should clean their classroom every week. I concede that it takes time from lessons, and some parents think the school should do it. Shop owners were especially worried, because they believed that fewer parking places would mean fewer customers. However, the figures published this spring tell a different story. Air quality has also improved, and the noise in the main streets has decreased. Several schools have reported that more pupils now come to class by bicycle. The researcher who led the study argues that the investment has already paid for itself, because the city now spends less on road repairs and on health care. She points out that sales in the shops along the new lanes have grown by six per cent. answer.text: Thank you, Tom. That is a valid point, and I agree with you up to a point. Phones do distract students, and nobody can deny it. But I see one drawback in a complete ban: many students use their phones to learn. For instance, last week my teacher asked us to record a short interview, and every group used a phone for it. Building on your idea, I would like to suggest a simple rule: phones stay in a box during explanations, and students can take them out when the teacher asks. Furthermore, we could ask the students to write the rules themselves. Seldom do people follow a rule that they did not help to make. Partly for that reason, I would not ban phones completely, but I would limit them clearly. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they need different rules? I would really like to hear your view before we decide anything.
accepted: Thank you, Tom. That is a valid point, and I agree with you up to a point. Phones do distract students, and nobody can deny it. Building on your idea, I would like to suggest a simple rule: phones stay in a box during explanations, and students can take them out when the teacher asks. Furthermore, we could ask the students to write the rules themselves. Seldom do people follow a rule that they did not help to make. Partly for that reason, I would not ban phones completely, but I would limit them clearly. Mia, what have you noticed with the younger children you work with? Do they need different rules? Thanks, Tom. That is a fair point, and I partly agree with you, because phones really do distract us in class. However, I see a drawback: some lessons need a phone, for example to look up a word or take a photo of the board. For instance, yesterday we used a phone to record our science experiment. Building on your idea, I would suggest that phones stay in a bag, and that the teacher decides when we can use them. Furthermore, students should help to make the rules, because we follow what we choose. This is a valid way to limit the problem without a complete ban. Mia, what do you see with your younger students? Would the same rules work for them? I am curious about your experience, and I would like to hear it before we decide.

answer.text: Last spring, I was in charge of the school recycling project. When I arrived, the bins were full because nobody had collected the paper for a week, and many students had stopped caring. My first step was to listen. I asked every class what was making recycling difficult, and most students said that nobody knew who was responsible. So I drew up a weekly rota and asked each class to choose a captain. I also wrote a short checklist for the captains, and I checked the bins myself every Friday during the first month. As a result, the bins have never been full again, and our recycling rate has doubled since then. Teachers have even started using the rota in other projects. The experience taught me that clear responsibility prevents most problems. It also taught me that a leader should listen before giving orders. Since then, I have used the same approach in every team I have joined.

As a result, the bins have never been full again, and our recycling rate has doubled since then. Teachers have even started using the rota in other projects. The experience taught me that clear responsibility prevents most problems. It also taught me that a leader should listen before giving orders. Two years ago, I was in charge of the charity concert at my school. When I joined the team, the posters were still not ready because nobody had booked the hall, and the students had already lost interest. I decided to start again with a clear plan. I made a checklist, I asked each class to choose a captain, and I called the music teacher to ask for help. We booked the hall within two days and sold every ticket in a week. As a result, the concert has become a yearly tradition, and the school has raised twice as much money since then. The experience taught me that a simple plan gives people confidence. I also learned that asking for help early saves time. Today, I use the same method whenever I start a new project.

answer.text: Thanks for having me. I am delighted to be your guest today. You asked what led me to start the volunteer club. Briefly, it began last year, when I was in charge of a small recycling project at school. When I arrived, nobody had emptied the bins for weeks, so I drew up a rota and asked each class to choose a captain. As a result, our recycling rate has doubled since then. You also asked about my biggest challenge. Honestly, it was keeping everyone interested. answer.text: I read the blog post about mobile phones and marks, and I think it has two important weaknesses. First, it seems to rely on a very small sample: the writer asked only five friends, so the result cannot speak for the whole school. Arguably, this is the main weakness, because five friends are not enough to prove anything. Second, the post is one-sided. It says the solution is to ban phones, but that is a false dilemma, because there are many other options. To some extent, the writer is right: the fall in marks may be linked to phones, and phones are likely to distract some students. However, a link is not proof, and other factors, such as stress or sleep, may account for the trend. A more balanced alternative would be to survey every class and then agree some simple rules, rather than ban everything. In my opinion, that would be fairer and more reasonable for everybody.

answer.text: I checked the viral story about the school closing, and I rate it as unproven. Second, the photo of the empty building is real, but it is misleading, because it was taken during last year's summer holidays, out of context. Third, the headline says most families have left, but it is based on a survey of only ten families, so it is a hasty generalisation. There is no evidence that the school will close, and the original source is missing. To find out more, we need the council's official report and the real number of students. Based on the evidence available, the story is likely to be false, although we may be wrong if new figures appear. In conclusion, readers should not share it until a reliable source confirms it.

answer.text: Should students have a say in the school rules? In this piece I will argue that they should. First, rules that nobody explains are rarely followed. When students help to write a rule, they understand the reason for it, and they respect it more. Second, taking part teaches responsibility. A student who helps to decide learns that every choice has consequences. I concede that students may not always choose the best rules. Nevertheless, teachers can guide the discussion, and, as mentioned above, a rule with a clear reason is easier to accept. This argument is stronger than the objection, because guided choices are still choices. Teachers and students want different things: the former want order, and the latter want fairness. A shared rule can give both. In conclusion, students deserve a voice in the rules they must follow, and the school will be calmer for it. Second, helping to make rules teaches responsibility, because a student learns that choices have consequences. Admittedly, some students will not choose wisely; nevertheless, teachers can guide them, and, as mentioned above, a clear reason makes any rule easier to accept. This argument answers the objection. answer.text: Our survey of two hundred pupils produced two main findings. First, sixty per cent of the pupils sleep less than eight hours a night. Second, among the pupils who sleep little, twice as many girls as boys say that they feel tired in class. These figures suggest that a lack of sleep may affect how pupils feel at school, and they appear to show that girls are more affected than boys. However, the results have an important limitation. All the pupils came from one school, and they described their own sleep, so the data may be biased. For this reason, we cannot say that sleep causes tiredness; we can only say that the two seem to be linked. Further research with a larger sample from several schools would be needed before we can speak for all teenagers. In short, the findings are interesting, but they should be read with care.
accepted: Our survey of two hundred pupils produced two main findings. First, sixty per cent of the pupils sleep less than eight hours a night. Second, among the pupils who sleep little, twice as many girls as boys say that they feel tired in class. These figures suggest that a lack of sleep may affect how pupils feel at school, and they appear to show that girls are more affected than boys. However, the results have an important limitation. All the pupils came from one school, and they described their own sleep, so the data may be biased. Further research with a larger sample from several schools would be needed before we can speak for all teenagers. In short, the findings are interesting, but they should be read with care.

We asked two hundred pupils about their sleep and found two things. To begin with, 60 per cent of them sleep for less than eight hours. In addition, among those pupils, double the number of girls compared with boys reported feeling tired during lessons. The data indicate that short sleep could be connected with tiredness in class, and girls seem to be more affected than boys. Nevertheless, there is a limitation: only one school took part, and the pupils described their own hours, so the answers may not be accurate. Because of this, the results do not prove a cause. More research with a larger sample from different schools would help to show whether the same pattern appears elsewhere. To sum up, the findings are useful, but they must be treated with care.

answer.text: Last June a survey was conducted among three hundred residents of the old neighbourhood. The participants were selected at random from a list and were asked to complete a questionnaire online. Two results stand out. First, roughly a third of the residents said that the street lighting is poor. Second, twice as many older residents as young ones feel unsafe at night. These findings suggest that lighting may be a priority for the neighbourhood, and they appear to show that older people are more worried. However, there is an important limitation: most answers came from two streets, and the residents described their own feelings, so the data may be biased. For that reason, we cannot generalise the results to the whole city. As a next step, we propose a three-month trial of new lamps in the two streets, and we suggest that the council should report the results in the autumn. Further research with a larger sample would then show whether the change really helped.
accepted: Last June a survey was conducted among three hundred residents of the old neighbourhood. The participants were selected at random from a list and were asked to complete a questionnaire online. Two results stand out. First, roughly a third of the residents said that the street lighting is poor. Second, twice as many older residents as young ones feel unsafe at night. These findings suggest that lighting may be a priority for the neighbourhood, and they appear to show that older people are more worried. However, there is an important limitation: most answers came from two streets, and the residents described their own feelings, so the data may be biased. For that reason, we cannot generalise the results to the whole city. As a next step, we propose a three-month trial of new lamps in the two streets, and we suggest that the council should report the results in the autumn. Further research with a larger sample would then show whether the change really helped.

We conducted a survey in June, and three hundred residents of the old town answered an online questionnaire. They were chosen at random from a local list. We found two main things. To begin with, about a third of the residents think the street lighting is bad. In addition, double the number of older people compared with young people feel unsafe when they walk at night. This indicates that better lighting could be a priority, and it seems that older residents are more concerned. Nevertheless, there is a limitation. Most of the answers came from two streets, and people only reported how they feel, so the results may not be reliable. We therefore cannot say that the same is true for the whole city. Our proposal is a trial of three months with new lamps in those streets, and we recommend that the council reports the results in the autumn. More research with a larger sample would show whether the trial helped.

prompt.es: Escucha la charla y resume tres ideas y dos detalles.

answer.text: The lecturer outlined three reasons why cities are planting more trees. According to her, the first reason is that trees cool the streets, and shade can make a street up to five degrees cooler in summer. The second reason is rain: the ground near a tree takes in more water, so there is less flooding after a storm. The third reason is that trees are good for people's minds, because residents who live near trees feel less stressed. She gave one example from a large city, where two thousand trees were planted along one street; after three years, the council reported that the street was noticeably cooler. She went on to give a detail about the costs: a young tree needs water every week for two years, and that costs money. To summarise, the lecturer said that trees are not a quick fix, but they are a good long-term investment.

The talk was about planting trees in cities. The speaker gave three main ideas. Firstly, trees make streets cooler, by up to 5 degrees in summer, because of the shade. Secondly, trees help when it rains, since the ground takes in water and there is less flooding. Thirdly, people who live near trees seem to feel less stress. As an example, she explained that two thousand trees were planted along one street in a large city, and three years later the street was cooler. She also mentioned a detail about the costs: young trees need water every week for two years, which is expensive for the council. In conclusion, the lecturer said that trees are not a quick solution, but they are a good investment for the future.

origin.audio: Today I want to talk about why cities are planting more trees. There are three main reasons. First, trees cool the streets. Shade can make a street up to five degrees cooler in summer. Second, trees help with rain. The ground near a tree takes in more water, so there is less flooding after a storm. Third, trees are good for people's minds. Studies suggest that residents who live near trees feel less stressed. One example comes from a large city, where two thousand trees were planted along one street. After three years, the council reported that the street was noticeably cooler. However, trees need care. A young tree needs water every week for two years, and that costs money. In short, trees are not a quick fix, but they are a good long-term investment.

prompt.es: Escucha el episodio y escribe un resumen con una implicación y tu reacción.

answer.text: In this episode, the host asked her guest whether it is better to work from home. According to the guest, it depends. First, many people save about two hours a day because they do not travel, and this is a real benefit. Second, some workers feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. Third, she said that companies could offer two office days a week, which she described as a good compromise. When the host asked whether working at home is better, she answered that it is not exactly better, which seemed to imply that the answer is not a simple yes. What struck me was that she never said it is easy. To be fair, I found the episode balanced. However, I would add one doubt: not everybody has a quiet room at home, so the benefits may be smaller for some people. I see her point, but I would like to hear more before I decide. In short, the episode was clear and useful, and I agree with her up to a point.

This episode of the podcast was about working from home. The host asked her guest if it is better, and the guest explained that it depends. On the positive side, many people save two hours a day because they do not travel to an office. On the negative side, some of them feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. She suggested that a good compromise could be two office days a week. The host asked again whether working at home is better, and the guest replied not exactly, which implied that the situation is more complicated than a simple yes or no. My reaction is positive: to be fair, she did not try to sell one answer. What struck me was how honest she was about the problems. However, I would add that some people do not have a quiet place at home, and that could make things harder for them. Overall, I agree with her up to a point, and I would like to hear how companies respond.

Every Sunday my grandfather used to fish at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother would laugh and say that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed, and the lake stayed as silent as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. "Unbelievable," he whispered. His hands shook a little as he held the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

Last year, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I understand that the budget is small, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. Let me put forward a proposal: a story workshop for the open day. When I was a child, the square used to be full of people, and I would love to see that again. Stories can bring neighbours together, and a simple workshop is a good way to start. Nobody needs a big stage to tell a story, only a few chairs and a little time. Fair enough, the budget is limited. Much as I would like a bigger stall, I am sure the volunteers can help, and I was wondering whether the library could lend us some books for the morning. answer.text: I would argue that schools should limit phones in class, but not ban them completely. For example, in my cousin's school the students keep their phones in a box during lessons, and the teachers say that the pupils now listen more carefully. Admittedly, phones can be useful: a dictionary, a map or a camera can help with a project. Much as I respect that view, the evidence I have seen points to another conclusion, because when a phone is on the desk, it is hard to ignore. The benefits depend on rules, or rather, on clear rules that everyone understands. What I mean is that the problem is not the phone itself but the moment when it is used. Schools could allow phones for specific tasks and keep them away during explanations and exams. Some parents worry about emergencies, so the school office should always be available by telephone. On balance, a limited and well-explained rule would help pupils to concentrate without feeling punished.
accepted: I would argue that schools should limit phones in class, but not ban them completely. For example, in my cousin's school the students keep their phones in a box during lessons, and the teachers say that the pupils now listen more carefully. Admittedly, phones can be useful: a dictionary, a map or a camera can help with a project. Much as I respect that view, the evidence I have seen points to another conclusion, because when a phone is on the desk, it is hard to ignore. The benefits depend on rules, or rather, on clear rules that everyone understands. What I mean is that the problem is not the phone itself but the moment when it is used. Schools could allow phones for specific tasks and keep them away during explanations and exams. Some parents worry about emergencies, so the school office should always be available by telephone. On balance, a limited and well-explained rule would help pupils to concentrate without feeling punished.

In my opinion, phones should stay in the bag during lessons. Take my own class: last year, we used to check messages all the time, and the teacher had to repeat every explanation twice. It is true that phones can help with research, and I do not want a total ban. Even though a quick search can save time, it also opens a hundred distractions. To put it more precisely, a phone is useful only when the teacher asks for it. Let me rephrase that: a phone is a tool, not a toy, and a tool needs a purpose. For instance, the class could use phones for a short quiz and then put them away. That is a fair compromise. Some students may feel nervous without their phones, but they would soon notice how much they can concentrate. All in all, a clear and limited rule is better than a total ban or complete freedom. Students need trust, and they also need help.

answer.text: Years ago, I used to believe that I would never speak English well. I had never spoken with a stranger in English, and I was afraid of making mistakes. Then I started studying with an app every morning, and my confidence slowly grew. The article says that students who learn with apps never speak well. Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and it gives no data about students who also talk with people, so its conclusion may not be reliable. I was wondering whether the author could explain how many students took part. I understand that a short article has little space, and I appreciate the concern about speaking well. Revision: I wrote that apps are useless for speaking, or rather, I should say that they are useful but not enough. On balance, the best plan is an app plus real conversations, and that is exactly what this course has given me.
accepted: Years ago, I used to believe that I would never speak English well. I had never spoken with a stranger in English, and I was afraid of making mistakes. When I was a child, I would watch films in English without understanding a word, and my cousin used to laugh at me. Later, I had to take an exam, and that was the moment when I decided to learn properly. An online post claims that apps are a waste of time. It is true that an app cannot replace a teacher. Even though I agree with part of that view, I think the post may be wrong, because it gives no numbers and does not say who wrote it. The source seems weak, so I would be careful before believing it. I was wondering whether the author has ever used an app for a full year. With respect, one experience does not prove a rule. I appreciate that some people learn better with a teacher, and I see your point. Let me rephrase my conclusion: apps do not teach everything, but they help you to start. In the end, I changed my opinion only a little, and this course helped me to explain why.
